refuted.fact: F10: 'Python 3.14+, uv, NVM, Node 24+, WSL 2+ Ubuntu, .NET 10 ... These six are the only entries in the whole chart that carry version markers, apart from PowerShell 7 in column 2.'
refuted.why: Contradicted by the chart I read myself at full resolution (3756x2292). Two of those six carry NO version marker at all: 'uv' and 'NVM' appear as bare names. The version-bearing entries in the whole chart are exactly five: Python 3.14+, Node 24+, WSL 2+ Ubuntu, .NET 10 (column 3) and PowerShell 7 (column 2). The six tool NAMES in column 3 are correct and confirmed; only the 'these six ... carry version markers' clause is wrong. A writer copying that sentence would invent versions for uv and NVM.

refuted.fact: sourcing_notes / not_said: 'Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, MSI, Intel, NVIDIA and Qualcomm are not mentioned in the Zenith post (grep: 0 matches for each).'
refuted.why: The grep claim is false for Intel: 'intel' occurs twice in the 2026-09-04 page text, in 'shifting some of that intelligence to the edge' and 'Windows Developer Configurations to Intelligent Terminal'. The substantive point survives - my word-boundary greps confirm Intel, HP, Lenovo, NVIDIA and Qualcomm never appear as company names and AMD is the only silicon partner named - but the record asserts a literal grep result that does not reproduce, and a later agent will re-run it.

unsupported.fact: F08: 'The actual pre-installed tool names appear ONLY in a chart image embedded in the post (alt text "Chart showing pre-installed tools", asset Preinstalled-tools-2.png).'
unsupported.why: Two problems, neither fatal. (a) The filename 'Preinstalled-tools-2.png' appears nowhere in the served HTML. I grepped the raw page: the only occurrence is 'Preinstalled-tools-2-1024x625.png', and there is no srcset. The bare filename is a WordPress size-suffix strip - a derived URL, not one reached from the page. It does resolve (200, 580,648 bytes) and serves the same chart, and F08-F10 are cited to the article URL rather than the image URL, so nothing is fabricated; but the note presents a derived URL as the official asset without saying it was derived, which is the exact habit the BRIEF bans. Record the on-page URL and state that the full-size variant was obtained by dropping the size suffix. (b) 'ONLY in a chart image' is overstated - the body text names Visual Studio Code and Windows Terminal. It is the complete 18-item list that exists only in the image.

unsupported.fact: F36: 'Micro Center is a United States retailer; AMD names no other region or retailer in this blog.'
unsupported.why: The second half is confirmed - AMD's page names no other retailer and no region. But 'Micro Center is a United States retailer' is nowhere on the AMD page; I searched the full extracted text. It is outside knowledge inserted into a fact record whose url is the AMD blog. Almost certainly true, but under the one-fact-one-fetched-url rule it cannot hang off that url, or the article will imply AMD said the launch was US-only.

unsupported.fact: F43: 'Both official Windows feeds are live and were used to confirm the date ... the windowsdeveloper feed returned 10 items with the newest dated 2026-09-14, and it lists the Zenith item as "Fri, 04 Sep 2026 10:00:29 +0000".'
unsupported.why: The content is correct - I reproduced it exactly - but the fact is attached to url = the article page, which contains none of it, and neither feed URL appears in `sources`. This is the one fact in the record that cannot be checked against its own cited url. Either attach the feed URL or move it into sourcing_notes, where it is already stated correctly, and drop it from verified_facts.

unsupported.fact: F21: the 2026-09-14 IFA post 'repeats the same device-class figures but writes the bandwidth as "250gbps" rather than "250+ GB/s".'
unsupported.why: Confirmed verbatim, but 'repeats the same figures' understates the divergence and must not travel into the article as written. The IFA post says '64GB+ unified memory and 250gbps memory bandwidth': it drops the plus sign from the bandwidth figure as well as changing the unit, and 250 gigabits per second is about 31 GB/s - a different quantity, not a different spelling. Quote only the 2026-09-04 form ('250+ GB/s'), and if the IFA wording is mentioned, say Microsoft wrote it inconsistently rather than treating the two as interchangeable.

additional_findings: MATERIAL OMISSION from the 2026-09-04 post: Microsoft explicitly says the hardware will differ between Zenith machines - 'By working with our OEM partners, we give developers choice across devices and performance tiers while preserving the ready-to-code experience. The hardware may vary, but the developer promise is consistent - powerful for modern development, thoughtfully configured and ready for developers from the start.' This is the only thing Microsoft says about what varies across Zenith devices and it speaks directly to the 'what IS Zenith' gap the researcher rightly flags as unanswered. Absent from all 43 facts.

MATERIAL OMISSION from the same post, the sentence immediately before the recorded 30B+ quote: 'Project Zenith devices come with a preconfigured Windows setup for development, and a set of tools curated for what developers reach first.' Microsoft's own one-line definition of the package, and the cleanest sentence to translate.

MATERIAL OMISSION from the Build 2026 post, and the best available answer to the reader question the researcher calls unanswerable ('can I get this without buying a machine?'): alongside the WinGet route in F26, Microsoft announced 'Windows 365 with Developer configuration - Windows 365 comes pre-configured with the same Windows developer configuration, available in public preview.' A cloud-PC route to the same configuration, in public preview as of 2026-06-02, with no hardware bar at all. Recorded nowhere.

MATERIAL OMISSION qualifying F33: the Build 2026 post's footnote [ii] reads 'Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box and Surface Laptop Ultra are pre-release products. Products and features are subject to regulatory certification/approval; actual sale and delivery is contingent on compliance with applicable requirements.' F33 records '128 GB unified memory' and 'available later this year in the U.S. exclusively on Microsoft.com' without it. If Dev Box availability is used, the caveat must travel with it.

UNDER-STATED in F22: the researcher flags 'GitHub Copilot CLI' vs the chart's 'GitHub Copilot', but the bigger point is that AMD's out-of-box list as relayed by Microsoft has FOUR items (Visual Studio Code, WSL, GitHub Copilot CLI, PowerShell) against Microsoft's eighteen, 'WSL' is not a chart entry at all (the chart says 'WSL 2+ Ubuntu'), and AMD's 'PowerShell' carries no version where the chart says 'PowerShell 7'. The AMD four-item list and the Microsoft eighteen-item chart must not be presented as the same thing.

NAMING TRAP inside AMD's own page, unflagged: the spec table row reads 'Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495' while footnote GRHP-01 reads 'Ryzen AI Max+ 495 PRO'. The researcher quoted each correctly in its own place (F38, F39) but never noted the clash, so a writer merging them will produce a product name that appears in neither.

CONTEXT the record misses on Microsoft's word 'unmetered': the Build 2026 post has a section headed 'Unmetered intelligence on Windows powered by on-device AI', announcing on-device SLMs 'Aion 1.0 Instruct' and 'Aion 1.0 Plan' as 'available in the coming months'. That is the origin of the Zenith post's 'locally and unmetered' framing, and it shows Microsoft's own local-model story was still forward-dated in June - which strengthens the researcher's correct refusal to attach any named model to the 30B+ claim.

I independently re-read the chart image at full resolution and confirm all 18 tool names and all three column headings exactly as recorded: 'Preinstalled tools'; 'Productivity & edit tools' = Visual Studio Code, GitHub Copilot, PowerToys, WinAppCLI, Windows Dev Skills (5); 'Terminal & source control' = Intelligent Terminal, PowerShell 7, Git, GitHub CLI, Azure CLI, Core Utils, Oh My Posh (7); 'Languages & runtimes' = Python 3.14+, uv, NVM, Node 24+, WSL 2+ Ubuntu, .NET 10 (6). This was the highest-risk item in the record and it holds up. F11's Windows Terminal / Intelligent Terminal inconsistency is real - the chart lists no 'Windows Terminal' anywhere.

I re-verified the AMD spec table cell by cell and every figure matches F39 exactly (495: 16C/32T, up to 5.2/3.1 GHz, 80 MB, Radeon 8065S, 45-120W, up to 55 TOPS, 40 CUs, 192 GB; 490: 12C/24T, 5.0/3.2, 76 MB, 8050S, 45-120W, 50 TOPS, 32 CUs, 192 GB; 485: 8C/16T, 5.0/3.6, 40 MB, 8050S, 45-120W, 50 TOPS, 32 CUs, 192 GB), including the GD-243 TOPS caveat and the GRHP-01 4-bit-quantization condition. The separation of the 128 GB / 200B Ryzen AI Halo from the 192 GB / 160 GB VRAM / 300B+ next-generation platform is correct and is the thing most likely to be re-merged by a careless writer.

I also machine-checked all 43 verbatim quotes against my own fetched text after normalising dashes, curly quotes and trademark symbols: every one matches the source. The only non-matches were the four expected cases - F01 (meta tags, verified separately in the raw HTML), F08-F10 (chart image, verified visually), and F43 (feed, verified against the feed).

No date conflation found. event_date 2026-09-04 is the announcement and publication date, corroborated by article:published_time, the visible dateline and two independent official feeds; article:modified_time 2026-09-04T13:17:30 is correctly treated as not moving the event date. Forward-dated items stay separate throughout: 'in the coming months' (more Zenith devices, undated), AMD pre-orders June 2026, AMD next-gen platform and OEM processor availability Q3 2026, and Build-2026 preview/GA labels explicitly scoped to 2026-06-02. The not_said warning that those preview/GA labels are as of June and not as of September is exactly right and must survive into the article. (One unrecorded detail: the Build post itself carries article:modified_time 2026-06-05T14:18:38, i.e. it was edited three days after publication.)

No disqualifying sourcing. All four `sources` are first-party (three Microsoft blogs, one AMD blog). Nothing in verified_facts traces to a news outlet, aggregator, law-firm blog or search snippet. The unverified_or_excluded list correctly quarantines the VideoCardz/Yahoo price claim - I confirm AMD's page contains no price and no '$' at all - and the search-snippet claim that merged the 128 GB/200B and 192 GB/300B products. Vendor-claim labelling is sound: performance and capability statements carry is_vendor_claim=true, and the false ones are page metadata (F01, F02), absence findings (F23, F34, F42) and the researcher's own observation of an internal inconsistency (F11). I found no vendor performance claim recorded as an independent fact.
